structure.rationale: The requester supplied eight numbered chapter headers, and they already form a sound teaching order: motivate the gap between chatting and acting, define the loop, then add one capability per chapter (tools, memory, guardrails) before the reader builds anything. Chapter 6 is the payoff — the first working agent — and is deliberately placed after the three capability chapters so the build is assembly rather than discovery. Chapters 7 and 8 are the two things that separate a demo from a system: coordination when one agent is not enough, and reliability engineering. One running example (a release-notes sidekick over a git repository) carries all eight chapters so no chapter spends its budget re-establishing a scenario.
structure.audience: Teen-to-adult beginner programmers and curious builders who can read Python but have not built an agent.

claims.text: A language model never executes anything on its own; it emits a structured request, and the application (or the provider's servers) runs the operation and returns the result into the conversation.
Tool use fits tasks the model cannot do from text alone: actions with side effects, fresh or external data, structured guaranteed-shape outputs, and calls into existing systems.
Tool use does not fit when the model can answer from training alone, when the interaction is one-shot Q&A with no side effects, or when tool-calling latency would dominate a trivial response.

Writing a regex to extract a decision from model output is a signal that the decision should have been a tool call — parsing free-form text to recover structured intent means the structure belongs in the schema.

pitfalls: Beginners assume the model runs the code it names; it only names it.
Reaching for an agent when a single API call would do adds latency and failure modes for no gain.

claims.text: The canonical agentic loop for client-executed tools is a while loop keyed on stop_reason: send a request with the tools array, receive stop_reason "tool_use" plus one or more tool_use blocks, execute each tool, send back tool_result blocks, and repeat while stop_reason is "tool_use".
The loop exits on any stop reason other than "tool_use" — "end_turn", "max_tokens", "stop_sequence", or "refusal".
Tool use is a contract: the application specifies what operations are available and what shape their inputs and outputs take, and the model determines when and how to call them.
Each request must carry the full prior conversation — the original messages, the assistant's response including its tool_use blocks, and a user message containing the tool_result blocks.
Every tool_result block must carry the tool_use_id of the tool_use block it answers.

snippets.note: The manual agentic loop, keyed on stop_reason. Verified against the documented loop shape.

pitfalls: Appending only the assistant's text instead of the full response.content drops the tool_use blocks and breaks the next request.
Breaking on stop_reason == 'end_turn' alone silently swallows 'max_tokens' and 'refusal'.

claims.text: Tools differ primarily by where the code executes, and there are three buckets: user-defined client tools, Anthropic-schema client tools, and server-executed tools.

Anthropic-schema client tools — memory, bash, text_editor, computer — have the same execution model as user-defined tools, but the schemas are trained-in, so the model calls them more reliably and recovers from errors more gracefully than it would with a custom equivalent.

For server-executed tools such as web_search, web_fetch, code_execution and tool_search, the application never constructs a tool_result block; the server-side loop runs the operation and feeds the output back before the response arrives.

The server-side loop has an iteration limit; if the model is still iterating when it hits the cap, the response returns stop_reason "pause_turn" instead of "end_turn", and the conversation must be re-sent to continue.
A tool definition consists of a name, a description, and an input_schema in JSON Schema form with typed properties and a required list.

With the default tool_choice of {"type": "auto"}, the model decides on each turn whether to call a tool or respond directly; it calls a tool when the request maps to that tool's described capability and the answer is not already in context.

Tool-triggering behavior is steerable from the system prompt: "Use the tools to investigate before responding" increases tool use, and "Use your judgment about whether to call a tool or respond directly" keeps triggering conservative.
Setting disable_parallel_tool_use to true inside tool_choice limits the model to at most one tool call per turn; by default a single assistant message may contain several tool_use blocks.
Adding strict: true to a custom tool definition guarantees that the model's tool calls match the declared schema exactly.
A tool failure is reported back as an ordinary tool_result with is_error set to true and the message in content, not as a dropped result.

Using tools adds input tokens: the tools parameter itself, the tool_use and tool_result blocks, and an automatically included tool-use system prompt that costs 286 tokens on Claude Opus 5 for tool_choice auto or none.

snippets.note: Error signalling on a tool result.

pitfalls: Vague descriptions are the most common cause of a tool never being called — the description is the trigger condition, not decoration.
Splitting parallel tool results across several user messages instead of returning them all in one.

claims.text: The memory tool lets a model store and retrieve information across conversations in a directory of memory files that persist between sessions, without keeping everything in the context window.

Memory supports just-in-time context retrieval: rather than loading everything up front, the agent records what it learns in files and reads them back on demand, which keeps the active context focused on the current task.
The memory tool is client-side — the model only requests file operations, and the application executes each request against storage it controls and returns the result in a tool_result block.
The entire tool configuration is the single entry {"type": "memory_20250818", "name": "memory"}; no input schema is defined for an Anthropic-provided tool, and no beta header is required.
The handler must implement six commands: view, create, str_replace, insert, delete, and rename.
The /memories path is a prefix the handler maps onto real storage, such as a per-user directory or keys in a database.

When the memory tool is present in the tools array, the API automatically adds a memory-protocol instruction to the system prompt telling the model to view its memory directory before doing anything else and to assume its context window may be reset at any moment.

A malicious path such as /memories/../../secrets.env can reach files outside the memory directory, so every path in every command must be validated: resolved to canonical form, checked to remain inside the memory root, and screened for traversal sequences including URL-encoded ones like %2e%2e%2f.

Context editing clears specific tool results on the client, while compaction summarizes the whole conversation server-side as it approaches the context window limit; long-running agents can use both alongside memory.

Recommended memory hygiene includes capping how large a file may grow, capping how many characters view returns and paging the rest with view_range, and periodically deleting files that have not been accessed in a long time.

In the multisession pattern, an initializer session sets up memory files before substantive work begins, later sessions open by reading them, and each session updates the progress log before it ends; a feature is marked complete only after end-to-end verification, not when the code is written.

snippets.note: The complete memory tool declaration — name must be "memory" and no input_schema is supplied.
Path-traversal guard following the documented safeguards: prefix check, canonical resolution, containment check.

pitfalls: Opening the requested path directly instead of resolving and containing it first.
Confusing conversation history (in-context, per-session) with memory (on disk, across sessions).
Letting memory files grow without bound until reading them costs more than re-deriving the facts.

claims.text: The model never executes anything itself, so every guardrail that matters is enforced in the harness that runs the tools, not in the prompt.
tool_choice accepts {"type": "auto"}, {"type": "any"}, {"type": "tool", "name": ...}, and {"type": "none"}, which is the mechanical control over whether a tool may be called at all.
Path validation is stated as the application's responsibility for file-touching tools: every path in every command must be checked, because the application executes whatever the model requests.

The model usually refuses to write sensitive information to memory files, but the documented recommendation for a stronger guarantee is validation in the handler that strips sensitive data before the file is written.
A refusal is a first-class outcome: "refusal" is one of the stop reasons the agentic loop can exit on, alongside "end_turn", "max_tokens", and "stop_sequence".
Returning an error to the model is done by setting is_error to true on the tool result and putting the message in content, which lets the model adapt rather than fail blindly.

pitfalls: Trusting a system-prompt rule to stop a destructive tool call; the prompt is a preference, the harness is the boundary.
Raising an exception on a bad tool input instead of returning an is_error tool_result, which denies the model any chance to recover.

claims.text: Claude Opus 5 has the model ID claude-opus-5, a 1M-token context window, 128k max output tokens, and pricing of $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens.

Claude Sonnet 5 has the model ID claude-sonnet-5, a 1M-token context window and 128k max output, at $3 per million input and $15 per million output tokens, with introductory pricing of $2/$10 per MTok through August 31, 2026.
Claude Haiku 4.5 has a 200k-token context window and 64k max output, at $1 per million input and $5 per million output tokens.
On Claude Opus 5 and Claude Sonnet 5 the effort parameter defaults to high on the Claude API, and must be set explicitly to use a different level.

The full round trip for a client tool is: first request carrying tools and the user message, a response containing a tool_use block naming the tool and its arguments, local execution, then a second request that sends the result back in a tool_result block so the model can answer.
The SDKs provide a Tool Runner that executes tools and sends the results back automatically, so the round trip does not have to be written by hand.

snippets.code:
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    tools=tools,
    tool_choice={"type": "auto", "disable_parallel_tool_use": True},
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What's the weather in San Francisco?"}],
)
tool_use = next(b for b in response.content if b.type == "tool_use")
snippets.note: First half of the documented round trip; the client resolves credentials from the environment.

snippets.code:
runner = client.beta.messages.tool_runner(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    tools=[memory],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Remember that Acme Corp prefers email follow-ups."}],
)
final_message = runner.until_done()
snippets.note: The SDK tool runner drives the loop; until_done() returns the final message.

pitfalls: Setting max_tokens too low, so the answer truncates and the loop has to be retried.
Hardcoding an API key instead of letting the client resolve credentials from the environment.

claims.text: The three execution buckets — user-defined client tools, Anthropic-schema client tools, and server-executed tools — determine which side of the boundary each unit of work runs on, which is the same question a multi-agent design has to answer for every specialist.

A server-executed tool already runs its own internal loop: the model searches, reads results, decides whether to search again, and iterates until it has what it needs, without the application participating.
The tool_search tool exists specifically for working with large tool libraries by discovering and loading tools on demand rather than holding every schema in context.
The advisor tool pairs a faster executor model with a higher-intelligence advisor model consulted mid-generation, which is a two-model division of labour available without building a coordinator.
Model choice is a real lever for delegation economics: Haiku 4.5 costs $1/$5 per MTok against Opus 5's $5/$25, so a cheap specialist and an expensive coordinator differ fivefold per token.

pitfalls: Adding a second agent before the single-agent loop is instrumented, so a coordination bug and a tool bug look identical.
Assuming subagents share context — each one starts from whatever its caller put in its messages.

claims.text: The loop must branch on every stop reason, not just success: "end_turn", "max_tokens", "stop_sequence", and "refusal" all exit the loop and mean different things.

A paused turn is not a failure: stop_reason "pause_turn" means the server-side loop hit its iteration cap and the conversation should be re-sent, including the paused response, to let the model continue where it left off.
Errors are returned to the model as tool_result blocks with is_error true rather than raised, which is what lets an agent retry or change approach instead of crashing.

Token cost is observable per request: the response reports input and output token counts in its usage metrics, and tool use adds the tools parameter, the tool_use and tool_result blocks, and a tool-use system prompt on top of the normal request.
Server tools can add usage-based charges beyond tokens, such as web search charging per search performed.

Model capabilities and token limits can be queried programmatically through the Models API, whose response includes max_input_tokens, max_tokens, and a capabilities object for every available model — so a harness can check limits at runtime instead of hardcoding them.
In the documented multisession pattern, a feature is marked complete only after end-to-end verification confirms it works, not when the code is written.
Reliable knowledge cutoffs are published per model — May 2026 for Claude Opus 5 and January 2026 for Claude Sonnet 5 — which bounds what an agent can answer without a retrieval tool.

snippets.note: Exhaustive stop_reason handling plus a hard iteration bound.

pitfalls: An unbounded while loop with no iteration cap, which turns one bad tool result into an unbounded bill.
Treating 'pause_turn' as an error and discarding a turn that was only partway through its own server-side loop.
